newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German committee bogged down on tax talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German committee bogged down on tax talks.

text.p: German politicians on Wednesday became bogged down in the details of scrapping a single business tax after admitting there was no hope of salvaging plans for a broad overhaul of the national tax system.

Parliament's mediation committee did not even manage to begin discussing Finance Minister Theo Waigel's tax-cutting plan, after two days of preliminary talks between the government and opposition Social Democrats (SPD) found no basis for agreement.
Instead, negotiators said they were edging towards a deal on abolishing a capital trading tax on companies after a row which has dragged on for over two years.
"I would have wished that this capacity to agree had been present over the great tax reform -- then we would have made a big leap forward," Waigel said during a break in the meeting.
The mediation committee is a last-ditch forum for clearing legislative roadblocks arising from the SPD's control of the Bundesrat upper house.
The SPD voted down Waigel's 30 billion mark ($16.3 billion) package of income and corporate tax cuts in early July.

Negotiations had been scheduled to wrap up at lunchtime, but dragged on into the early evening as the two sides wrangled over constitutional changes and financing models for the capital trading tax's abolition.
Although a deal on that issue still appeared possible, both sides said it was clear no agreement was possible on systemic tax reform before general elections in the autumn of next year.
"We have negotiated for weeks and the positions are unchanged," SPD chief whip Peter Struck told German Radio. "We have to expect that there will be no tax reform before 1998."
Thuringia state premier Bernhard Vogel, from Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), also said he saw no chance of agreement on an SPD proposal to lighten the cost of employing workers.

The SPD wants to cut unemployment and pensions insurance charges by a percentage point each from this October in a bid to reduce payroll costs and cut record post-war unemployment now at over four million.
"I don't expect mediation on the tax reform to succeed, nor on the non-wage costs, but I am still hopeful of a common agreement on the capital trading tax," Vogel said.

Business leaders and economists poured scorn on Bonn's tax paralysis -- which has been overshadowed by a cross-party balanced budget and tax-cutting deal struck by U.S. Democrats and Republicans this week.
Hans-Olaf Henkel, head of the Federation of German Industry (BDI), has already said Germany's failure to shake up its tax system would condemn it to the second division of world economic powers.
Rolf Peffekoven, a member of the 'five wise men' panel of independent government economic advisors, called the failure of the tax reform "a bitter setback for Germany".

"Top tax rates would have had to be cut to restore our country's competitiveness," he told Radio Bremen television. "The concept was definitely right, even if the financing had not been thought through properly."
Gerhard Grebe, economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, told Reuters the cost of the failure of the tax reform could be half a percentage point in growth per year in the longer term.

"We are stuck in a reform logjam and now all important reforms will be postponed until after the elections," he said. "The tax reform would have been a signal abroad we could reform the system. Now I expect more firms to move jobs abroad."
Rejection of the tax plans will send them back to the Bundestag lower house, which is expected to pass them again at a special sitting next Tuesday.

They will then go before the Bundesrat, which is likely to rejected them again at a meeting in early September, raising the prospect of parliament's mediation committee meeting all over again in the autumn.
-- douglas.busvine@reuters.com (Bonn 49-228-26097 150) ($ = 1.837 German Marks)
